newsitem.title: GERMANY: German FDP rules out tax hikes to plug deficit.
newsitem.headline: German FDP rules out tax hikes to plug deficit.

text.p: A junior German coalition partner of Chancellor Helmut Kohl, the liberal Free Democrats (FDP), reaffirmed on Friday their opposition to any increase in taxes to cover a tax revenue shortfall of 18 billion marks ($10.6 billion).

The FDP's tough stance is one factor leaving the coalition with a lack of options that prompted Finance Minister Theo Waigel to propose on Thursday revaluing the Bundesbank's gold reserves to help to plug the gap.

FDP general secretary Guido Westerwelle dismissed speculation that Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) and Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union (CSU), would go ahead and raise taxes against the FDP's wishes.
"State income is insufficient precisely because taxes are too high," Westerwelle told a news conference presenting the resolutions to be approved at its party congress next week.
"We must lower taxes so that more people can be employed and are contributing taxes once again," he said, attacking the high non-wage labour costs German employers are obliged to pay.

"The coalition has agreed there will be no more tax hikes. We are now in a difficult budgetary situation, but we still believe raising tax would be a gigantic mistake and detrimental to the economy as a whole," Westerwelle said.
Westerwelle's comments coincided with a flurry of comments from FDP leaders, all ruling out tax hikes, a day after Waigel revealed the new budget gap and his gold revaluation scheme.
Both FDP chief Wolfgang Gerhardt and a former economics minister, the FDP's Otto Lambsdorff, said raising taxes were not a solution despite the desperate situation.

The FDP, which barely wins the five percent of votes needed to stay in parliament, is torn between its free-market tax-cutting platform and loyalty to the other coalition partners, who have contemplated tax hikes to solve Germany's budgetary crisis.

Westerwelle said that in the current crisis more new debt would be an acceptable solution to ward off the threat of mass unemployment as well as an acceleration of the government's privatisation programme.
He stressed that the FDP wanted less public debt and more private initiative.
"State finances are under strain, the individual is not challenged enough. We have too much state stagnation and not enough personal initiative," he said. "But a credit would be the lesser evil."

Westerwelle said the FDP wanted to cut new net borrowing to zero in the next 10 years and to ban this in the long term. This would one of the party's key resolutions to be voted on at the congress in Wiesbaden.
The FDP, according to opinion polls, has between five and six percent support -- and looks set to struggle for survival before elections in 1998.
"The situation in the jobs market pushes us towards any (budgetary) measure that does not involve tax increases," FDP chief Gerhardt said in a statement.
